answer.answer: Audit-ready takeover completed and persisted as checkpoint `checkpoint:f3f22633-f0e6-368e-66bc-bf14f42de743`. No second canonical snapshot was created.

claims.value: `Star Rupture Game Analysis.zip` was preserved losslessly: 21,674,717 bytes, SHA-256 `1a1c1ef0ae00905ced37f1221ab22c4b9268f2ebe17b7516e6c9cac67d7f6fa3`, with 123 archive entries. `unzip -t` passed and all 115 manifested files passed SHA-256 verification. The original ZIP and verified extraction remain under Git-ignored `raw/`; tracked `MANIFEST.csv` and `CHECKSUMS.sha256` retain the audit trail.

The archive’s numeric data is not proven to be Steam build `23761620`; that identifies only the latest public executable it observed: Hotfix `0.2.8`. The correct boundary has two axes: game data claims Update 1 internal version `35118973`, dated 2026-04-09 and contextually mapped to Steam build `22674441`/inferred `0.2.0`; the canonical source capture is SRDB `2.3.4`, snapshot `ea-u1-gv35118973__srdb-2.3.4__20260711T050230Z`, retrieved 2026-07-11 05:02:30 UTC. Archive reports remain July 8 legacy calculations until ported and rerun against that canonical snapshot.

The archive’s 468 items, 191 public buildings, 234 recipe definitions, 77 Corporation levels, 121 export offers, 15 upgrades, 3,259 map markers, 3,094 loot rows, and official-news subset duplicated the richer corpus and were not installed as a competing snapshot. Selectively promoted material comprised the player save baseline `models/rourke-update1-save-baseline__20260711.json`; six medium-confidence Ore Excavator v2 recipe-producer associations; explicit medium-confidence consumable-effect assumptions with provenance warnings; nine player-specific site/geography assets; and consolidated player-save, architecture, geography, progression, exploration, food, and remote-resource notes. Reconciliation also corrected the overwritten `airlock` detail and Training Corporation’s literal `$undefined` index.

The complete 18-file `Flowworks Campaign Sizing - Levels 8 to 15` family is superseded audit history and must not become current guidance; its buffer-heavy, three-Stabilizer/two-slow-press direction was rejected. The July 11 adopted plan—guidance, not confirmed construction—starts with one Stabilizer, one Impeller, and one Turbine; expands with one Nozzle and two Valves; later adds two Pumps; defers the second Stabilizer until before Scanner/levels 11–12; and reserves HRS v2 only if imported-HRS recovery fails in practice. The canonical corpus and active RuptureOps pipeline/database remain authoritative; the archive’s SQLite database, source JSON, delivery CSVs, workbook, refresh script, and query script remain preserved only under `raw/`.

answer.answer: The first Geo Scanner became a durable lesson in recovery planning: powered defenses and an independent safe recovery cache are essential, while the corruption mechanic and loot details remain deliberately unresolved.

claims.value: The first Geo Scanner required three attempts. Death one respawned the player at a nearby claimed base, but it lacked spare weapons and replacement materials, forcing a walk to Landerworks. On attempt two, the scanner fire base’s claimed Regeneration Chamber was available, but its turrets were unpowered and did nothing; the player was overwhelmed, infection/corruption disabled the base and chamber, and the player respawned at the starting launcher. Attempt three succeeded with a fully built-out fire base and every turret powered.

The successful intervention was to fully build out the temporary fire base, power every turret, and verify defenses before activation. The automated defense completed the scanner encounter, and the player found hearing the turrets “sing” against the enemy highly satisfying.

Direct observation establishes only this encounter’s sequence: unpowered turrets provided no defense, then infection/corruption disabled the contested base and its claimed Regeneration Chamber. It does not establish a universal corruption threshold or complete rules governing when Regeneration Chambers become unavailable.

For future scanners: claim a nearby Regeneration Chamber but assume it may fail; power every turret and verify tracking/firing before activation; place at least one replacement weapon kit, ammunition, healing, and basic rebuilding materials in a separate safe cache outside the contested base’s failure area; preserve a route to a stable base or launcher; and treat activation as a deliberate defense event. The completed scanner appeared to yield two particularly good food-related rewards or stacks, possibly involving a quantity of 20, but their exact identities and counts remain unresolved because the dictated report was ambiguous.

checkpoint.objective: Incorporate the player’s first Geo Scanner experience into durable operational guidance.
current_state: Failure chain, successful intervention, evidence boundary, future checklist, and loot ambiguity are verified.
decisions: Treat the encounter as direct historical observation.
Do not generalize it into a universal corruption or Regeneration Chamber mechanic.
Preserve the ambiguous loot report without inventing item names or counts.
open_questions: What were the exact identities and counts of the two food-related rewards or stacks?
What universal conditions or thresholds, if any, disable a Regeneration Chamber?
next_actions: Use the fire-base and independent-cache checklist for future scanner activations.
Confirm scanner identity and loot details during a live refresh.
Require repeatable evidence before promoting a universal chamber-disable rule.

answer.answer: RuptureOps can presently be released only as a corpus-free implementation build. All third-party data, personalized material, and retained media must stay private pending permission or licensed replacements.

claims.value: SRDB permits crawling but provides no explicit data/content reuse license. Its raw mirror, normalized snapshots/corpus, derived SQLite database, mirrored assets, and duplicate third-party data in imports are private research material and cannot be redistributed publicly without separate permission.

Private personalized material includes all three user-authored prompt dumps, conversation-derived decisions, imported package contents, player save state, play-history models, player-specific vault notes, screenshots, and site/geography artifacts such as world-map-named-sites.png, world-map-named-sites.svg, and its required world-map-overview.png. Only non-content manifests and promoted provenance-labeled facts are eligible for version control; that does not itself authorize public redistribution.

A public build can use the original RuptureOps implementation and project scaffolding: the current configuration defines an iOS 17.0, Swift 6.0 RuptureOps application plus unit-test and UI-test targets. It must be corpus-free and use only original or separately cleared placeholder assets. It must not bundle the source datasets, imports, player artifacts, nine site/geography assets, other binary site images, generated app icon, or warning audio. Consequently, corpus-backed reference and personalized features are not presently cleared for public distribution.

Before broader distribution, obtain explicit reuse permission from the source owner covering redistribution, derivatives, and mirrored assets, or adopt a separately licensed data strategy using official/openly licensed, independently recreated, or user-entered data. Separately remove or obtain consent for personalized imports, save/history models, screenshots, maps, images, the generated icon, and warning audio; replace uncleared media with original or explicitly licensed assets, then audit the release bundle to confirm none of the private raw, normalized, SQLite, imported, player-specific, or binary material is included.

Which original or explicitly licensed replacement images, icon, audio, and data will be selected?
